title: Computational Analysis of Character Development in Holocaust Testimonies
measurement_description: The paper measures the ability of Large Language Models to extract and classify the evolution of a protagonist's 'religious trajectory' (changes in disposition toward religious belief and practice) along a narrative timeline. Specifically, it evaluates LLM performance in classifying the valence of religious practice (Active, Inactive, Other, None) and religious belief (Positive, Negative, Other, None) within first-person Holocaust survivor testimonies.
findings: The study identified common sequences in the religious trajectories of Holocaust survivors: for belief, a constant positive disposition was the most common (45%), while for practice, most trajectories (68%) presented an oscillating structure. When evaluating LLMs, the authors found a 'positivity bias,' where models tended to overpredict positive categories for belief and active categories for practice. Furthermore, the models exhibited stereotype biases rooted in pretraining; for example, they predicted Christian prayers with a positive valence even when the study's specific annotation guidelines defined non-Jewish religious expressions as carrying a negative valence.
